Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yeah 😄 — 5% CPU for an audio control panel is unnecessarily high, especially if the UI is mostly sitting idle. And if it feels laggy, I'd optimize it before adding more features.

Based on the code we've already seen, I strongly suspect the culprit is the polling architecture, not React/Vite itself.

What I'd optimize first

Your current flow appears to be roughly:

Timer
  ↓
snapshot()
  ↓
decodeDevices()
  ↓
PowerShell → registry
  ↓
getPnP()
  ↓
PowerShell → Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity
  ↓
send data to renderer
  ↓
React re-render

If that happens frequently, you're repeatedly starting PowerShell processes and querying Windows hardware. That's expensive.

🚀 Biggest improvement

Instead of doing this every few hundred milliseconds:

snapshot()
 ├─ PowerShell registry query
 └─ PowerShell CIM query

I'd split it into different update frequencies:

                 ┌── UI state ───────────── every ~250-500 ms
                 │
snapshot ────────┤
                 │
                 ├── Current codec/bitrate ── every ~500 ms
                 │
                 └── PnP hardware scan ───── every ~5-10 sec

The PnP information almost never changes.

There's no reason to repeatedly execute:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive
Memory:         modest

rather than the current ~5%.

And since you already have the application functioning, this is a good time to optimize it before we pile more features on top.

If you paste your current src/main/main.ts and src/renderer/main.tsx, I can go through the actual code and point out exactly where the CPU/lag is coming from and give you the replacements rather than guessing.

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yep — now it's a different, very specific issue. The cast is being parsed incorrectly.

You have:

PowerShell
[Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal][Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent().IsInRole(...)

PowerShell is calling .IsInRole() on the WindowsIdentity, instead of first converting it to WindowsPrincipal.

Fix isAdmin() one more time

In:

src\main\main.ts

replace the whole function with:

TypeScript
function isAdmin() {
  if (MOCK) return true;
  try {
    const result = ps(
      '$p = New-Object Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal([Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()); $p.IsInRole([Security.Principal.WindowsBuiltInRole]::Administrator)'
    );
    return /True/i.test(result);
  } catch {
    return false;
  }
}

This avoids PowerShell's cast ambiguity entirely by explicitly creating a WindowsPrincipal.

Then:

PowerShell
Ctrl+C
npm run build
npm run dev

Why this should work

The PowerShell code is now explicitly:

PowerShell
$p = New-Object Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal(
    [Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()
)

$p.IsInRole(
    [Security.Principal.WindowsBuiltInRole]::Administrator
)

So .IsInRole() is definitely being called on WindowsPrincipal, which is the class that actually provides that method.

The repeated messages should also disappear because snapshot() is apparently polling this function repeatedly.

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yeah 😄 — 5% CPU for an audio control panel is unnecessarily high, especially if the UI is mostly sitting idle. And if it feels laggy, I'd optimize it before adding more features.

Based on the code we've already seen, I strongly suspect the culprit is the polling architecture, not React/Vite itself.

What I'd optimize first

Your current flow appears to be roughly:

Timer
  ↓
snapshot()
  ↓
decodeDevices()
  ↓
PowerShell → registry
  ↓
getPnP()
  ↓
PowerShell → Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity
  ↓
send data to renderer
  ↓
React re-render

If that happens frequently, you're repeatedly starting PowerShell processes and querying Windows hardware. That's expensive.

🚀 Biggest improvement

Instead of doing this every few hundred milliseconds:

snapshot()
 ├─ PowerShell registry query
 └─ PowerShell CIM query

I'd split it into different update frequencies:

                 ┌── UI state ───────────── every ~250-500 ms
                 │
snapshot ────────┤
                 │
                 ├── Current codec/bitrate ── every ~500 ms
                 │
                 └── PnP hardware scan ───── every ~5-10 sec

The PnP information almost never changes.

There's no reason to repeatedly execute:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive
Memory:         modest

rather than the current ~5%.

And since you already have the application functioning, this is a good time to optimize it before we pile more features on top.

If you paste your current src/main/main.ts and src/renderer/main.tsx, I can go through the actual code and point out exactly where the CPU/lag is coming from and give you the replacements rather than guessing.

If that happens frequently, you're repeatedly starting PowerShell processes and querying Windows hardware. That's expensive.

🚀 Biggest improvement

Instead of doing this every few hundred milliseconds:

snapshot()
 ├─ PowerShell registry query
 └─ PowerShell CIM query

I'd split it into different update frequencies:

                 ┌── UI state ───────────── every ~250-500 ms
                 │
snapshot ────────┤
                 │

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive

rather than the current ~5%.

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yeah 😄 — 5% CPU for an audio control panel is unnecessarily high, especially if the UI is mostly sitting idle. And if it feels laggy, I'd optimize it before adding more features.

Based on the code we've already seen, I strongly suspect the culprit is the polling architecture, not React/Vite itself.

What I'd optimize first

Your current flow appears to be roughly:

Timer
  ↓
snapshot()
  ↓
decodeDevices()
  ↓
PowerShell → registry
  ↓
getPnP()
  ↓
PowerShell → Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity
  ↓
send data to renderer
  ↓
React re-render

If that happens frequently, you're repeatedly starting PowerShell processes and querying Windows hardware. That's expensive.

🚀 Biggest improvement

Instead of doing this every few hundred milliseconds:

snapshot()
 ├─ PowerShell registry query
 └─ PowerShell CIM query

I'd split it into different update frequencies:

                 ┌── UI state ───────────── every ~250-500 ms
                 │
snapshot ────────┤
                 │
                 ├── Current codec/bitrate ── every ~500 ms
                 │
                 └── PnP hardware scan ───── every ~5-10 sec

The PnP information almost never changes.

There's no reason to repeatedly execute:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive
Memory:         modest

rather than the current ~5%.

And since you already have the application functioning, this is a good time to optimize it before we pile more features on top.

If you paste your current src/main/main.ts and src/renderer/main.tsx, I can go through the actual code and point out exactly where the CPU/lag is coming from and give you the replacements rather than guessing.

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yep — now it's a different, very specific issue. The cast is being parsed incorrectly.

You have:

PowerShell
[Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal][Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent().IsInRole(...)

PowerShell is calling .IsInRole() on the WindowsIdentity, instead of first converting it to WindowsPrincipal.

Fix isAdmin() one more time

In:

src\main\main.ts

replace the whole function with:

TypeScript
function isAdmin() {
  if (MOCK) return true;
  try {
    const result = ps(
      '$p = New-Object Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal([Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()); $p.IsInRole([Security.Principal.WindowsBuiltInRole]::Administrator)'
    );
    return /True/i.test(result);
  } catch {
    return false;
  }
}

This avoids PowerShell's cast ambiguity entirely by explicitly creating a WindowsPrincipal.

Then:

PowerShell
Ctrl+C
npm run build
npm run dev

Why this should work

The PowerShell code is now explicitly:

PowerShell
$p = New-Object Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal(
    [Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()
)

$p.IsInRole(
    [Security.Principal.WindowsBuiltInRole]::Administrator
)

So .IsInRole() is definitely being called on WindowsPrincipal, which is the class that actually provides that method.

The repeated messages should also disappear because snapshot() is apparently polling this function repeatedly.

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yeah 😄 — 5% CPU for an audio control panel is unnecessarily high, especially if the UI is mostly sitting idle. And if it feels laggy, I'd optimize it before adding more features.

Based on the code we've already seen, I strongly suspect the culprit is the polling architecture, not React/Vite itself.

What I'd optimize first

Your current flow appears to be roughly:

Timer
  ↓
snapshot()
  ↓
decodeDevices()
  ↓
PowerShell → registry
  ↓
getPnP()
  ↓
PowerShell → Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity
  ↓
send data to renderer
  ↓
React re-render

If that happens frequently, you're repeatedly starting PowerShell processes and querying Windows hardware. That's expensive.

🚀 Biggest improvement

Instead of doing this every few hundred milliseconds:

snapshot()
 ├─ PowerShell registry query
 └─ PowerShell CIM query

I'd split it into different update frequencies:

                 ┌── UI state ───────────── every ~250-500 ms
                 │
snapshot ────────┤
                 │
                 ├── Current codec/bitrate ── every ~500 ms
                 │
                 └── PnP hardware scan ───── every ~5-10 sec

The PnP information almost never changes.

There's no reason to repeatedly execute:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive
Memory:         modest

rather than the current ~5%.

And since you already have the application functioning, this is a good time to optimize it before we pile more features on top.

If you paste your current src/main/main.ts and src/renderer/main.tsx, I can go through the actual code and point out exactly where the CPU/lag is coming from and give you the replacements rather than guessing.

Yep 😄 — slight UI lag is probably okay for now, especially since you're running a development build:

PowerShell
npm run dev

You have Vite + Electron + a periodic PowerShell/device scan running simultaneously. That can make things feel less smooth.

A few things could be causing it:

  • snapshot() is probably polling frequently and calling PowerShell commands.

  • Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity can be relatively slow.

  • Electron's renderer and main process communicate through IPC.

  • You're running Vite in development mode, which has extra overhead.

One thing I'd check

Your snapshot() appears to call:

TypeScript
decodeDevices()
getPnP()

every time it runs. getPnP() executes:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...

If you're doing that every few hundred milliseconds, that's likely the source of the lag.

So I wouldn't worry about optimizing it yet. First make sure the application actually works correctly.

If the UI is responsive but just has a little delay when devices update, that's quite normal for this architecture.

Once everything works, we can make it much smoother by, for example, polling PnP less frequently and caching the result, while keeping the UI updates fast.

Ahh, yes — now that I know exactly which project you're building, your idea makes sense.

According to the reverse-engineering notes in the repo, the license is enforced by the GUI, not by AltA2DP.sys itself. The notes say the trial is 7 days, while the kernel driver has no license check. GitHub+1

So conceptually there are two separate things:

  1. Which driver Windows is using

    • Microsoft's BthA2dp.sys

    • or Luculent's AltA2DP.sys

  2. Whether the official AltA2DP GUI considers your license valid

    • trial

    • paid

    • expired/no license

The important part is that an expired trial does not inherently mean Windows automatically switches the driver back. The README specifically describes switching back as a separate PnP/driver-store operation: removing/uninstalling the AltA2DP driver causes Windows to fall back to its inbox BthA2dp.sys. GitHub

Your custom app could therefore be designed like this

                 Your app
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          │                   │
    Windows A2DP         Alternative A2DP
       mode                    mode
          │                   │
    Microsoft driver       AltA2DP.sys
                              │
                         Your settings
                         / codec config

And I'd actually make the UI explicit:

Driver

  • 🟢 Windows A2DP

  • 🔵 Alternative A2DP

rather than trying to make "license expired" silently change things.

For example:

Alternative A2DP
────────────────────────
Driver:       Active ✓
License:      Expired
Codec:        LDAC

[ Switch to Windows A2DP ]

Then if the user clicks it, your application performs the legitimate driver/PnP transition.

And yes, you can have Windows mode as the fallback

That is actually a pretty sensible design.

Your app could detect:

AltA2DP driver installed?
        │
       yes
        │
License/config usable?
   ┌────┴────┐
  yes       no
   │          │
 AltA2DP    Windows

But: I would not make your app inspect or manipulate the vendor's license to get around the expiration. You don't need to. Your app can simply treat the license state as unavailable and offer Windows A2DP as a fallback.

The repo itself documents that the driver switch is independent of the GUI licensing mechanism. GitHub

And honestly, given what we've built so far, I'd add this as the next feature: a "Switch to Windows driver" / "Switch to Alternative A2DP" control, with the current driver shown clearly. That would also make your app much more useful if AltA2DP isn't available for some reason.

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yeah 😄 — 5% CPU for an audio control panel is unnecessarily high, especially if the UI is mostly sitting idle. And if it feels laggy, I'd optimize it before adding more features.

Based on the code we've already seen, I strongly suspect the culprit is the polling architecture, not React/Vite itself.

What I'd optimize first

Your current flow appears to be roughly:

Timer
  ↓
snapshot()
  ↓
decodeDevices()
  ↓
PowerShell → registry
  ↓
getPnP()
  ↓
PowerShell → Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity
  ↓
send data to renderer
  ↓
React re-render

If that happens frequently, you're repeatedly starting PowerShell processes and querying Windows hardware. That's expensive.

🚀 Biggest improvement

Instead of doing this every few hundred milliseconds:

snapshot()
 ├─ PowerShell registry query
 └─ PowerShell CIM query

I'd split it into different update frequencies:

                 ┌── UI state ───────────── every ~250-500 ms
                 │
snapshot ────────┤
                 │
                 ├── Current codec/bitrate ── every ~500 ms
                 │
                 └── PnP hardware scan ───── every ~5-10 sec

The PnP information almost never changes.

There's no reason to repeatedly execute:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive
Memory:         modest

rather than the current ~5%.

And since you already have the application functioning, this is a good time to optimize it before we pile more features on top.

If you paste your current src/main/main.ts and src/renderer/main.tsx, I can go through the actual code and point out exactly where the CPU/lag is coming from and give you the replacements rather than guessing.

Yeah 😄 — 5% CPU for an audio control panel is unnecessarily high, especially if the UI is mostly sitting idle. And if it feels laggy, I'd optimize it before adding more features.

Based on the code we've already seen, I strongly suspect the culprit is the polling architecture, not React/Vite itself.

What I'd optimize first

Your current flow appears to be roughly:

Timer
  ↓
snapshot()
  ↓
decodeDevices()
  ↓
PowerShell → registry
  ↓
getPnP()
  ↓
PowerShell → Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity
  ↓
send data to renderer
  ↓
React re-render

If that happens frequently, you're repeatedly starting PowerShell processes and querying Windows hardware. That's expensive.

🚀 Biggest improvement

Instead of doing this every few hundred milliseconds:

snapshot()
 ├─ PowerShell registry query
 └─ PowerShell CIM query

I'd split it into different update frequencies:

                 ┌── UI state ───────────── every ~250-500 ms
                 │
snapshot ────────┤
                 │
                 ├── Current codec/bitrate ── every ~500 ms
                 │
                 └── PnP hardware scan ───── every ~5-10 sec

The PnP information almost never changes.

There's no reason to repeatedly execute:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive
Memory:         modest

rather than the current ~5%.

And since you already have the application functioning, this is a good time to optimize it before we pile more features on top.

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yeah 😄 — 5% CPU for an audio control panel is unnecessarily high, especially if the UI is mostly sitting idle. And if it feels laggy, I'd optimize it before adding more features.

Based on the code we've already seen, I strongly suspect the culprit is the polling architecture, not React/Vite itself.

What I'd optimize first

Your current flow appears to be roughly:

Timer
  ↓
snapshot()
  ↓
decodeDevices()
  ↓
PowerShell → registry
  ↓
getPnP()
  ↓
PowerShell → Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity
  ↓
send data to renderer
  ↓
React re-render

If that happens frequently, you're repeatedly starting PowerShell processes and querying Windows hardware. That's expensive.

🚀 Biggest improvement

Instead of doing this every few hundred milliseconds:

snapshot()
 ├─ PowerShell registry query
 └─ PowerShell CIM query

I'd split it into different update frequencies:

                 ┌── UI state ───────────── every ~250-500 ms
                 │
snapshot ────────┤
                 │
                 ├── Current codec/bitrate ── every ~500 ms
                 │
                 └── PnP hardware scan ───── every ~5-10 sec

The PnP information almost never changes.

There's no reason to repeatedly execute:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive
Memory:         modest

rather than the current ~5%.

And since you already have the application functioning, this is a good time to optimize it before we pile more features on top.

If you paste your current src/main/main.ts and src/renderer/main.tsx, I can go through the actual code and point out exactly where the CPU/lag is coming from and give you the replacements rather than guessing.

oh also maybe you could like optimize our contraption, yeah it does look cool! ...even better than that one, but its laggy... and eats 5% cpu...

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yeah 😄 — 5% CPU for an audio control panel is unnecessarily high, especially if the UI is mostly sitting idle. And if it feels laggy, I'd optimize it before adding more features.

Based on the code we've already seen, I strongly suspect the culprit is the polling architecture, not React/Vite itself.

What I'd optimize first

Your current flow appears to be roughly:

Timer
  ↓
snapshot()
  ↓
decodeDevices()
  ↓
PowerShell → registry
  ↓
getPnP()
  ↓
PowerShell → Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity
  ↓
send data to renderer
  ↓
React re-render

If that happens frequently, you're repeatedly starting PowerShell processes and querying Windows hardware. That's expensive.

🚀 Biggest improvement

Instead of doing this every few hundred milliseconds:

snapshot()
 ├─ PowerShell registry query
 └─ PowerShell CIM query

I'd split it into different update frequencies:

                 ┌── UI state ───────────── every ~250-500 ms
                 │
snapshot ────────┤
                 │
                 ├── Current codec/bitrate ── every ~500 ms
                 │
                 └── PnP hardware scan ───── every ~5-10 sec

The PnP information almost never changes.

There's no reason to repeatedly execute:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive
Memory:         modest

rather than the current ~5%.

And since you already have the application functioning, this is a good time to optimize it before we pile more features on top.

If you paste your current src/main/main.ts and src/renderer/main.tsx, I can go through the actual code and point out exactly where the CPU/lag is coming from and give you the replacements rather than guessing.

oh also maybe you could like optimize our contraption, yeah it does look cool! ...even better than that one, but its laggy... and eats 5% cpu...

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yeah 😄 — 5% CPU for an audio control panel is unnecessarily high, especially if the UI is mostly sitting idle. And if it feels laggy, I'd optimize it before adding more features.

Based on the code we've already seen, I strongly suspect the culprit is the polling architecture, not React/Vite itself.

What I'd optimize first

Your current flow appears to be roughly:

Timer
  ↓
snapshot()
  ↓
decodeDevices()
  ↓
PowerShell → registry
  ↓
getPnP()
  ↓
PowerShell → Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity
  ↓
send data to renderer
  ↓
React re-render

If that happens frequently, you're repeatedly starting PowerShell processes and querying Windows hardware. That's expensive.

🚀 Biggest improvement

Instead of doing this every few hundred milliseconds:

snapshot()
 ├─ PowerShell registry query
 └─ PowerShell CIM query

I'd split it into different update frequencies:

                 ┌── UI state ───────────── every ~250-500 ms
                 │
snapshot ────────┤
                 │
                 ├── Current codec/bitrate ── every ~500 ms
                 │
                 └── PnP hardware scan ───── every ~5-10 sec

The PnP information almost never changes.

There's no reason to repeatedly execute:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive
Memory:         modest

rather than the current ~5%.

And since you already have the application functioning, this is a good time to optimize it before we pile more features on top.

If you paste your current src/main/main.ts and src/renderer/main.tsx, I can go through the actual code and point out exactly where the CPU/lag is coming from and give you the replacements rather than guessing.

oh also maybe you could like optimize our contraption, yeah it does look cool! ...even better than that one, but its laggy... and eats 5% cpu...

Програма ChatGPT сказала:

Yeah 😄 — 5% CPU for an audio control panel is unnecessarily high, especially if the UI is mostly sitting idle. And if it feels laggy, I'd optimize it before adding more features.

Based on the code we've already seen, I strongly suspect the culprit is the polling architecture, not React/Vite itself.

What I'd optimize first

Your current flow appears to be roughly:

Timer
  ↓
snapshot()
  ↓
decodeDevices()
  ↓
PowerShell → registry
  ↓
getPnP()
  ↓
PowerShell → Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity
  ↓
send data to renderer
  ↓
React re-render

If that happens frequently, you're repeatedly starting PowerShell processes and querying Windows hardware. That's expensive.

🚀 Biggest improvement

Instead of doing this every few hundred milliseconds:

snapshot()
 ├─ PowerShell registry query
 └─ PowerShell CIM query

I'd split it into different update frequencies:

                 ┌── UI state ───────────── every ~250-500 ms
                 │
snapshot ────────┤
                 │
                 ├── Current codec/bitrate ── every ~500 ms
                 │
                 └── PnP hardware scan ───── every ~5-10 sec

The PnP information almost never changes.

There's no reason to repeatedly execute:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive
Memory:         modest

rather than the current ~5%.

And since you already have the application functioning, this is a good time to optimize it before we pile more features on top.

If you paste your current src/main/main.ts and src/renderer/main.tsx, I can go through the actual code and point out exactly where the CPU/lag is coming from and give you the replacements rather than guessing.

                 └── PnP hardware scan ───── every ~5-10 sec

The PnP information almost never changes.

There's no reason to repeatedly execute:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity

while you're sitting there listening to music.

Even better: cache PnP

Something like:

TypeScript
let cachedPnP: any[] = [];
let lastPnPScan = 0;

function getPnP() {
  if (MOCK) {
    return MOCK_DEVICES.map(d => ({
      DeviceID: d.instanceId,
      Name: d.name,
      Status: d.current?.opened ? 'OK' : 'Unknown'
    }));
  }

  const now = Date.now();

  if (now - lastPnPScan < 5000) {
    return cachedPnP;
  }

  const script = `Get-CimInstance Win32_PnPEntity ...`;
  const data = ps(script, { json: true });

  cachedPnP = data
    ? (Array.isArray(data) ? data : [data])
    : [];

  lastPnPScan = now;
  return cachedPnP;
}

That alone could make a huge difference.

And there's another optimization

Don't send the entire state to React if nothing changed.

Currently you're effectively doing:

Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
Windows → snapshot → IPC → React
...

even when absolutely nothing changed.

We can keep the previous snapshot:

TypeScript
let previousSnapshot = '';

const next = JSON.stringify(snapshot());

if (next !== previousSnapshot) {
  previousSnapshot = next;
  mainWindow.webContents.send('snapshot', JSON.parse(next));
}

So React only receives an update when something actually changed.

🎨 Then optimize the renderer

If the UI is still slightly laggy after fixing the polling, we'd look at your main.tsx.

Things I'd specifically check:

  • unnecessary whole-page React re-renders

  • setInterval inside React components

  • effects being recreated

  • expensive .map() operations

  • state being updated even when values haven't changed

  • animations running continuously

  • IPC listeners being registered more than once

One important thing

Don't optimize by just reducing the polling interval to something huge.

For example:

❌ 5 seconds for everything

would save CPU but make codec/bitrate changes feel slow.

Instead:

Fast:
  connection/current codec state

Slow:
  PnP/device discovery

Event-driven:
  settings changes

That's the architecture I'd aim for.

Target

I'd consider something around:

Idle CPU:       ~0–1%
UI interaction: smooth
Device scan:    occasional
Codec updates:  responsive
Memory:         modest

rather than the current ~5%.

And since you already have the application functioning, this is a good time to optimize it before we pile more features on top.
